Aaron Levie of @Box on why AI widens the gap between experts and everyone else, and what that means for college students:

"The biggest gains of AI go to people who have some degree of expertise in an area, to know what is actually true, what is not gonna work, 'What should I integrate from the output of this AI?'"

"If you don't have a deep understanding of your particular space or field or domain, you aren't able to then have the right judgment to make all of those decisions."

"So I think the experts just get more powerful in this world."

"I'm not even convinced that you can tell a college student to learn anything different than any other period in history. Be really good at a particular field, and then AI is merely a turbocharger of your capability in that particular field."

@levie

BREAKING: Japanese banks sold -$16 billion of foreign bonds in September, their largest monthly sale since February.

This also marks their 9th consecutive monthly sale, the longest streak since 2022.

As a result, sales of foreign debt by Japanese banks in the first 9 months of 2026 were the largest for that period since 2005.

Japanese financial institutions have turned to domestic government bonds, whose yields have surged to their highest levels in 3 decades.

Over the 5 months ending in August, large banks and insurers bought +$34 billion of Japanese government bonds with maturities of 2 years or more, their largest 5-month purchase since the start of 2023.

Global bond demand is undergoing a historic shift as yields rise.

tweets.text:
Global smartphone purchases have collapsed.

Worldwide smartphone shipments dropped -22.0% YoY in Q3 2026, to 255.3 million units, their largest quarterly decline on record.

Samsung's shipments fell -5.8% YoY, to 57.8 million units, while Apple's declined -4.0% to 57.3 million units.

At the same time, Xiaomi shipments fell -29.2% YoY to 30.7 million units, Oppo dropped -34.5%, to 25.6 million units, while Vivo fell -31.5%, to 19.1 million units.

This comes as memory costs have surged +350% since last year, driven by AI-related demand, putting further pressure on smartphone manufacturers.

As a result, soaring component costs are forcing vendors to raise prices and reduce budget-focused offerings, with consumers increasingly keeping their existing devices for longer.

Global smartphone sales are contracting amid surging prices.

tweets.text:
Ben Horowitz on the two skills that will matter more than ever before in an AI world: creativity and relationships.

"I think those are things that are hard to get out of today's AI in a very good way. So if you don't have instincts around those things, I don't know if all the AI in the world could help you. Whereas the grind-them-out tasks, AI is already really good at."

"Do you have original ideas? Can you establish and maintain very high quality, high fidelity relationships with people off the rip? I think people don't think about that enough."

"One big advantage I think that we have is we really look for that. Many just ignore that whole thing, like it's not a thing... It's a thing."

@bhorowitz w/ @Tocelot

Trucks haul the majority of US freight by weight, around 11.5 billion tons a year, and that load is projected to climb toward 15 billion by 2040. The industry employs about 2.2 million drivers and still runs a chronic shortage. Aurora expects 200 driverless 18-wheelers on Texas highways, with rivals close behind.

This is where AI reaches the real economy: the largest single expense in hauling every physical good you buy.

$AUR

🚨 🇺🇲 The US bond market is starting to say the trillions of dollars promised to build its infrastructure could become impossible to finance under current conditions and I think we are witnessing a genuine regime shift.

📊 For three years, markets have rewarded companies announcing the most spectacular investment plans, but now investors are finally starting to ask the right questions. Who is financing these projects? At what cost? With what guarantees? For what return? 47 major data center projects have been delayed, canceled, or blocked in 2026, while only 35% of the US data center pipeline is actually credible according to Bernstein. We are talking about a potential investment wave exceeding $10 trillion between 2025 and 2032 - FT

📉 Companies developing these infrastructures must spend billions upfront to purchase GPUs, build data centers and secure electricity supplies, while the associated revenues may not materialize for several years. Their entire business model depends on their ability to keep raising capital at reasonable costs, but that assumption is currently being challenged. CoreWeave lost 25% last week while some of its bonds suffered a sharp sell-off as the market is wondering whether these projects are financially viable at all.

➡️ Few other examples to understand. Cipher agreed to absorb the first $359 million in cost overruns on one project, creating an additional equity requirement of $750 million. Nscale has a contract potentially worth $45 billion with Anthropic but Anthropic can walk away if certain financing or delivery commitments are not met. Meanwhile, SB Energy needs around $174 billion in capital to fulfill contracts representing $430 billion in future revenue, despite not having completed a single data center. Some companies are being valued on enormous contracts without having demonstrated that they can actually finance and deliver the infrastructure behind them.

⚠️ We also need to revisit the circular financing structure of this industry which I have discussed before. Nvidia invests in companies that buy its chips, AI labs sign contracts that allow developers to raise debt, and SPVs or private credit funds finance infrastructure based on expected future revenues. As long as capital keeps flowing, the system works, but if investors suddenly demand much higher yields, the entire mechanism can start breaking down. Projects get delayed, GPU orders are postponed, developers face financial difficulties, and creditors reassess their exposure. A financing crisis can trigger an investment crisis before demand for AI even starts slowing down and many people tend to forget that. Moreover, that risk is concerning given how important AI-related investment has become as a driver of US economic growth.

📈 I do not think we are witnessing the collapse of the entire industry. Instead, we may be entering a much more brutal selection process between financially viable projects and those built on unrealistic assumptions. Lower Fed rates will not solve the problem as if credit spreads widen faster than risk-free rates decline, the overall cost of financing will continue to rise.

💸 I maintain that we need to return to a cost of capital and valuation levels that are consistent with the actual economic profitability of these projects. The technological success of AI does not guarantee financial success for the companies funding its infrastructure. History has already taught us this through railroads, telecommunications, and the internet. A technology can revolutionize the economy while destroying enormous amounts of investor capital.

The current tensions in the bond market are a serious warning sign ⚠️

*FT link: https://t.co/7McdVBF6nk

Weather is a commodity input. A strong El Nino this long is a supply risk sitting under every food and energy price.

Price shocks fade. Money printing is what embeds inflation, and that is the number that actually matters. A Fed that hikes into an energy spike is fighting the wrong war.

The other periods you can see here are: (working backwards) 20/21, 09, 03, 91,  and 87. Each beta unwind preceded a peak in eco/eps growth and breadth. Stock prices = outcome - expectations. My 2c.
